title: Valuation topology and common nontrivial coarsenings
statement: Let $K$ be a field and let $v_i:K\to\Gamma_i\cup\{\infty\}$ for $i=1,2$ be two nontrivial additive valuations, with surjective value groups $\Gamma_i=v_i(K^\times)$. Thus $v_i(0)=\infty$, $v_i(xy)=v_i(x)+v_i(y)$, and $v_i(x+y)\geq\min(v_i(x),v_i(y))$. Put $V_i=\{x:v_i(x)\geq0\}$ [def-trf-valuation-ring] and give $K$ the topology whose basis is $\{x:v_i(x-a)>\gamma\}$, for $a\in K$ and $\gamma\in\Gamma_i$. These two topologies are equal if and only if there exists a valuation ring $U\subsetneq K$ with $V_1\cup V_2\subseteq U$. Such a $U$ is called a common nontrivial coarsening. This does not assert $V_1=V_2$. No henselian, rank-one, or completeness hypothesis is imposed.

proof.text: For each $i$, the valuation inequalities make $V_i$ a subring of $K$. For $x\ne0$, $v_i(x^{-1})=-v_i(x)$, so either $x\in V_i$ or $x^{-1}\in V_i$. Nontriviality supplies $\varepsilon_i>0$ in $\Gamma_i$: negate a nonzero value if necessary. Surjectivity then supplies an element of value $-\varepsilon_i$, outside $V_i$. Thus $V_i\ne K$. Write $B_i(\gamma)=\{x:v_i(x)>\gamma\}$; in particular $B_i(0)\subseteq V_i$, so $V_i$ is a neighbourhood of zero.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed p.374, valued-field background; elementary agent proof of the common-coarsening topology criterion (not stated there).

proof.text: Assume the two topologies agree. Since $V_1$ is a zero-neighbourhood, the stated ball basis supplies $\delta\in\Gamma_2$ with $B_2(\delta)\subseteq V_1$. Choose $a\in K^\times$ with $v_2(a)=\delta+\varepsilon_2$. For $y\in V_2$, the product formula gives $v_2(ay)\ge\delta+\varepsilon_2>\delta$ (including $y=0$), hence $aV_2\subseteq V_1$.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed p.374, valued-field background; elementary agent proof of the common-coarsening topology criterion (not stated there).

proof.text: Let $S\subseteq K$ consist of all finite sums $\sum_{r=1}^n x_r y_r$ with $x_r\in V_1$, $y_r\in V_2$, allowing the empty sum. It is a subring: concatenate sums for addition, negate the $x_r$ for negatives, and distribute products to obtain terms $(x_rx_s^\prime)(y_ry_s^\prime)$. It contains both $V_1$ and $V_2$ by taking the other factor to be $1$. Moreover $aS\subseteq V_1$, since each $a x_r y_r=x_r(ay_r)$ belongs to $V_1$ by Step 2. If $S=K$, multiplication by $a\ne0$ gives $K=aK=aS\subseteq V_1$, contradicting Step 1. Thus $S\subsetneq K$.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed p.374, valued-field background; elementary agent proof of the common-coarsening topology criterion (not stated there).

proof.text: For $z\in K^\times$, Step 1 puts either $z$ or $z^{-1}$ in $V_1\subseteq S$. This also shows that $K$ is the fraction field of $S$: either $z=z/1$ or $z=1/(z^{-1})$, with numerator and nonzero denominator in $S$. The subring $S$ is an integral domain because it is contained in a field. The characterization in [def-trf-valuation-ring] therefore makes $S$ a valuation ring with fraction field $K$. Taking $U=S$ proves the common proper coarsening assertion.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed p.374, valued-field background; elementary agent proof of the common-coarsening topology criterion (not stated there).

proof.text: Conversely suppose a proper valuation ring $U\subsetneq K$ contains $V_1\cup V_2$. Choose $t\in K\setminus U$; then $t\ne0$. For either $i$ and every nonzero $u\in U$, one has $v_i(u)>v_i(t)$. Otherwise $v_i(t/u)=v_i(t)-v_i(u)\ge0$, so $t/u\in V_i\subseteq U$, and closure of $U$ under multiplication would give $t=(t/u)u\in U$, a contradiction. The same strict inequality holds for $u=0$, whose value is $\infty$. Thus $U\subseteq B_i(v_i(t))$ for both $i$.

source.place: XX 4.4, printed p.374, valued-field background; elementary agent proof of the common-coarsening topology criterion (not stated there).

proof.text: Fix distinct $i,j\in\{1,2\}$ and a threshold $\gamma\in\Gamma_i$. Choose $b\in K^\times$ with $v_i(b)=\gamma-v_i(t)+\varepsilon_i$. Step 5 implies $bU\subseteq B_i(\gamma)$. Since $V_j\subseteq U$, one also has $B_j(v_j(b))\subseteq bV_j\subseteq bU$: for nonzero $z$ in that ball, $v_j(z/b)>0$, and zero belongs as well. Consequently $B_j(v_j(b))\subseteq B_i(\gamma)$. Translating by any centre $c\in K$ gives a $j$-ball about $c$ inside each $i$-ball about $c$. Every open set in topology $i$ is therefore open in topology $j$. Interchanging $i,j$ proves equality of the two topologies. No comparison of ranks, equality of valuation rings, or Archimedean property was used.
